title: Semantic & Metrics Layer
summary: Five dashboards, five slightly different definitions of "active user." A metrics layer fixes that by defining each metric once, in code, and making every tool query through it instead of redefining it.

slides.markdown:
Every well-run warehouse eventually hits the same failure: two dashboards report different numbers for something that sounds unambiguous, like "active users," and nobody can immediately say which one is right — because both were built correctly against slightly different definitions.

A **semantic layer** (or metrics layer) is the fix: define each metric exactly once, in version-controlled code, and have every BI tool, notebook, and report query through that single definition instead of re-deriving it from raw tables. It turns "what does active mean" from a recurring argument into a single answered question.

"Active user" sounds like a fact. In practice, every team that builds a dashboard makes an independent judgment call: does it mean logged in in the last 7 days, or 30? Does a bot account count? Does a user who only opened a push notification without engaging count as active?

Five teams, five dashboards, five reasonable-sounding definitions — and the moment someone tries to reconcile a growth report against a finance report, the numbers don't match, for reasons that have nothing to do with a data quality bug. The data is correct in each dashboard; the *definitions* silently diverged.

slides.sectionTitle: A metrics layer as a version-controlled definition
slides.markdown:
A metrics layer defines each metric as code — typically YAML or a small DSL, committed to a repository, reviewed like any other change. "Active user" becomes one file that says exactly what it counts, with a name, an owner, and a git history showing every time the definition changed and why.

Every consumer — a BI dashboard, a notebook, an ad-hoc SQL query through the layer's API — asks for `active_users` by name and gets back the same computed value, because they're all hitting the same definition, not re-deriving their own SQL against raw event tables. Changing the definition means changing it once, reviewed once, and every downstream consumer picks up the new definition automatically the next time they query.

Every consumer sits above the semantic layer, never querying raw tables directly for a defined metric — the layer is the single point that resolves "active_users" into an actual SQL query against the warehouse.

slides.sectionTitle: The primitives a metric is built from
slides.markdown:
Metrics layers compose from a small set of primitives that map directly onto dimensional modeling vocabulary:

- **Measure** — the underlying additive quantity, usually a column on a fact table (`session_count`, `revenue`).
- **Dimension** — what you can slice or filter the metric by (`region`, `signup_cohort`, `plan_tier`).
- **Grain** — the level the metric is computed at (`per user per day`, `per account per month`).

A metric definition is really just: take this measure, apply this filter and this time window, and expose the result sliceable by these dimensions. "Active users" becomes `COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) WHERE last_active_at >= NOW() - 7 days`, defined once, exposed with `region` and `plan_tier` as available slice dimensions.

slides.sectionTitle: Headless BI vs each tool defining its own metrics
slides.markdown:
| | Each BI tool defines metrics | Headless BI / metrics layer |
|---|---|---|
| Where definitions live | Inside each BI tool's own config, siloed | One shared, version-controlled layer |
| Consistency across tools | Not guaranteed — Looker's "active user" can differ from Tableau's | Guaranteed — every tool queries the same definition |
| Review process | Often none — a dashboard author edits a calculated field directly | Code review, same as any other pipeline change |
| Switching BI tools | Re-implement every metric in the new tool | Point the new tool at the existing layer, definitions carry over |

"Headless BI" means the metrics layer is the source of truth and any visualization tool is a replaceable front end — the opposite of metrics living trapped inside one tool's proprietary config.

slides.sectionTitle: A metric quietly redefined in a new dashboard
slides.markdown:
Without a metrics layer, this happens constantly: an analyst builds a new dashboard, needs "active users," and — rather than hunting down whether an official definition exists somewhere — writes a reasonable-looking `COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)` filtered to their own idea of "active." It's close to the official number. It's just not the same number.

The dashboard ships, looks correct, and quietly disagrees with the "official" active-user metric by a few percent. Nobody notices until an executive puts both numbers side by side in the same meeting — at which point it looks like a data quality failure, when the real cause is that no shared, enforced definition existed for the analyst to find and reuse in the first place.

A typical metrics-layer definition, in the style used by tools like dbt's Semantic Layer or Cube:

```yaml
metrics:
  - name: active_users
    description: Users active in the trailing 7 days, excluding bot accounts
    type: count_distinct
    measure: user_id
    filter: "last_active_at >= current_date - interval '7 days' AND is_bot = false"
    dimensions: [region, plan_tier, signup_cohort]
```

Any consumer requesting `active_users` sliced by `region` gets a query generated from this single source, not from whatever SQL they happened to write. Changing the trailing window from 7 to 14 days is a one-line pull request, reviewed once, that updates the number everywhere it's used.

slides.sectionTitle: Adoption is the hard part, not the tooling
slides.markdown:
The technical piece of a metrics layer is usually the easy part — the tooling to define and serve metrics is mature and well-documented. The hard part is organizational: getting every existing dashboard migrated off ad-hoc SQL and onto the shared layer, and getting new dashboards built through it by default rather than by habit.

A metrics layer with three metrics defined and forty dashboards still bypassing it entirely provides almost none of its promised value — the inconsistency it's meant to prevent is still happening in the other forty. The rollout that actually works starts with the highest-traffic, most-disputed metrics first (usually revenue and active-user variants), proves the consistency win concretely, and only then expands coverage — rather than trying to model every metric in the business before anyone gets to use it.

A junior answer to "why would you build a metrics layer" is "so numbers match." A senior answer names the actual mechanism: definitions move from scattered, ungoverned SQL inside individual dashboards to a single, version-controlled, reviewed artifact that every consumer resolves against — turning a social problem (five teams silently disagreeing) into an engineering one (one file, one review process, one source of truth).

That reframing — governance as code, not tribal knowledge — is the real point, and it's the same instinct behind data contracts and data catalogs, covered elsewhere in this area: make agreements explicit and enforced, not assumed and eventually violated.
